title: The unborn
hook: Bankei taught ordinary people: you already have the unborn Buddha-mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bassui's question: when a sound comes, who is hearing? Your line: stay with the not-finding. Which sound became a bell for you? Day one thousand three.

A man comes to a Zen teacher with a confession. I was born with a short temper, he says. It's just how I am. How do I fix it? The teacher looks interested. That's remarkable, he says. Show it to me. The man says he can't, not right now. It only comes out sometimes, when something sets it off. Then, says the teacher, it isn't something you were born with. You make it, on the spot. The teacher was Bankei, and he told plain stories like this to ordinary people. Today, the unborn.
screen: `I WAS BORN THIS WAY.` → `SHOW IT TO ME.` → `YOU MAKE IT ON THE SPOT.`

segments.voice: Bankei was a Japanese Rinzai Zen teacher, and his teaching fits in a sentence. Everyone already has the Buddha-mind, and it is unborn. First, unborn. Bankei means a mind that was never produced, never put together, so it can never fall apart. It's what's here before you start building moods and grudges and stories. He says everything is handled perfectly well by it, without your adding anything. Second, ordinary people. Bankei spoke in everyday Japanese, not in the scholar's Chinese of the sutras. Records of his talks show farmers, townspeople, women and men, monks and lay people coming to listen. He mostly skipped the old koan stories and talked about their actual lives: anger, worry, sleepiness, the neighbors. Third, how the unborn gets lost. In the temper story, nobody is born angry. Something happens, you want your own way, and you turn the unborn mind into a fighting mind. Bankei calls that trading the Buddha-mind for something smaller. Don't fight the anger with more effort, he says. Just don't make it. Stay unborn. Fourth, trust. Bankei was wary of teachers who told students to strain and grind for awakening. So his advice is gentle: you already have it. Stop swapping it for something else. On an ordinary day, the unborn sounds like this: the kettle clicks off, and you just hear it. Someone cuts in line, and for one beat, before the story starts, there's only seeing.
screen: `THE BUDDHA-MIND IS UNBORN.` · `PLAIN WORDS FOR ORDINARY PEOPLE.` · `NOBODY IS BORN ANGRY.` · `YOU ALREADY HAVE IT.` · then, large: `STAY UNBORN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like: trust your ordinary mind. Sit however is comfortable. Don't try to make anything happen. Notice that seeing is already happening without your effort: light, shapes, the room. Feeling is already happening: the seat, the air, the breath. You didn't build any of it. When a thought starts building something, a plan, a complaint, a worry, notice the building, and don't add the next brick. Come back to what's already working fine on its own. Nothing to earn here. The bell holds the time.
The unborn. Bankei's word for the Buddha-mind everyone already has, never produced, so it never falls apart. Today's word.
Your line: the kettle clicks off. Today, when irritation starts to rise, catch the beat before it, and see if you can leave the irritation unmade. Day one thousand three.

howItsDone: Zen students and teachers read Bankei's recorded talks and point to the unborn mind in everyday life; his way is often taught without koans, as trusting the mind that is already working.

original.note: Japanese fusho: unborn, Bankei's word for the Buddha-mind.

trapdoor: what you thought: something about life before birth.
what it means: the Buddha-mind everyone already has, never produced, never falling apart.
what a scholar hears: Bankei's teaching of the unborn, given in plain Japanese talks and often taught without koans.

notes: No public-domain translation of Bankei on the validator's list; all paraphrased.
The short-temper story is from Bankei's recorded sermons; confirm the paraphrase.
'Records of his talks show farmers, townspeople, women and men' and 'mostly skipped the old koan stories': general claims, confirm or soften.
His illness from early striving is framed as tradition; confirm.
Romanized term fusho and kanji 不生 to confirm (Bankei's full phrase is fusho no busshin, the unborn Buddha-mind).
The kettle and line-cutting images are illustrations, not from the text.
Bankei's well-known example of hearing a crow or sparrow during a talk was left out to avoid repeating yesterday's hearing angle.
Editor: cut Bankei's illness from early striving (and its myth item) so it does not repeat day 1006's Hakuin illness story three days later.
